speaking.instruction: Record 60–90 seconds for each task. You may re-record once. Audio is evaluated on Fluency, Pronunciation, Confidence and Grammar (AI rubric).

tasks.label: Speaking Task 1
tasks.prompt: Describe a technical challenge you overcame in a team project. What was the problem, your role, the steps you took, and the outcome? Speak for 60–90 seconds.

tasks.label: Speaking Task 2
tasks.prompt: Explain an AI tool you use as a developer. How do you verify that its output is correct before using it? Speak for 60–90 seconds.

reading.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Questions test inference, detail and vocabulary — not just keyword matching.
reading.passage: When AI coding assistants moved from novelty to daily tooling, many teams assumed engineer productivity would rise uniformly. Evidence has been less tidy. A twelve-month study across forty firms compared 2,200 engineers split by their verification behaviour. High verifiers, who routinely read generated code, wrote regression tests and traced edge cases before merging, shipped features 34% faster with a 24% lower defect escape rate than a control group without tooling. Low verifiers, by contrast, were 14% faster to first commit but 18% more likely to introduce post-release defects, and their work took longer to review because teammates could not distinguish reviewed from un-reviewed generated code. The authors argue that the bottleneck of software engineering has shifted from code production to code verification: the scarce skill is no longer producing plausible implementations, but judging whether they are correct, secure and appropriate. Firms that treated the tools as mere accelerators saw most gains erode within two quarters, while those that rewrote their review rituals, such as mandatory tests for generated blocks and an explain-before-merge rule, sustained gains and reported higher junior confidence. None of the firms eliminated human review; the strongest results came from pairing the assistant with tight, fast feedback loops.

questions.question: What most accurately describes the study's overall finding?
options: AI tools uniformly improved every team
Productivity gains depended heavily on engineers' verification behaviour
Juniors benefited most from skipping review
Defect rates were identical across groups
questions.answer: Productivity gains depended heavily on engineers' verification behaviour

questions.question: What characterised 'low verifiers'?
options: Slow first commits and few defects
Fast first commits but more post-release defects
They wrote the most regression tests
questions.answer: Fast first commits but more post-release defects

questions.question: The phrase 'the bottleneck … shifted from code production to code verification' implies:
options: The key skill is judging correctness rather than generating code
Code review is no longer needed
questions.answer: The key skill is judging correctness rather than generating code

questions.question: Why did low verifiers' code take longer to review?
options: Teammates could not tell reviewed from un-reviewed generated code
The code was written in unfamiliar languages
questions.answer: Teammates could not tell reviewed from un-reviewed generated code

questions.question: Which practice was part of the firms that sustained gains?
options: Mandatory tests for generated blocks and explain-before-merge
Sharing one assistant login per team
questions.answer: Mandatory tests for generated blocks and explain-before-merge

questions.question: What can be inferred about human review in the strongest-performing firms?
options: It was removed in favour of the assistant
It was paired with tight, fast feedback loops alongside the assistant
It was done by external auditors
questions.answer: It was paired with tight, fast feedback loops alongside the assistant

writing.instruction: Write 150–300 words. You are assessed on Clarity, Grammar, Structure and Professional tone by an AI rubric.
writing.scenario: You are a junior developer. A third-party payments API your product depends on suffered an outage, delaying a committed feature by 3 days. Write an email to the client explaining the delay, its impact, what your team is doing about it (mitigation), and the revised, realistic timeline. Tone: professional, accountable, solution-oriented — not defensive.

Pseudocode: s=0; for i in 1..5: s = s + (i % 2 == 0 ? i : 0). What is printed?

nested loops: for i in 1..n: for j in i..n: constant work. Complexity?

options: Treat as promising but confirm with a larger sample
Reject the variant because p is small
problem.answer: Treat as promising but confirm with a larger sample

debugging.title: Python — Off-by-one in pagination
debugging.buggy:
def paginate(items, page, size):
    start = page * size
    end = start + size
    return items[start:end]  # page=1 should return the FIRST page

# paginate(list(range(20)), 1, 5) currently returns [5,6,7,8,9]
debugging.prompt: Fix pagination so page=1 returns the first page. Also handle page < 1, size <= 0, and requests beyond the last page without crashing. You may use AI — write the corrected function.
debugging.hint: Consider zero-based indexing and input validation.

debugging.title: JavaScript — Race condition / duplicate fetches
debugging.prompt: Fix so concurrent calls with the same key trigger fetcher() exactly once and all callers receive the same value. Handle a failing fetch by removing the in-flight entry so a retry is possible.
debugging.hint: Cache the in-flight Promise, not just the resolved value.

debugging.title: Python — Mutating a list while iterating
debugging.prompt: Rewrite so every inactive user is removed safely without skipping elements or raising. Preserve order of the remaining users. Explain the root cause in a comment.
debugging.hint: Build a new list, or iterate over a copy / indices in reverse.

feature.title: Feature: Build a sliding-window rate limiter
feature.spec: You are adding API protection to an existing Node/Express service. Implement an in-memory sliding-window rate limiter: function isAllowed(userId, maxRequests = 5, windowMs = 60000). It returns true if the user has made fewer than maxRequests within the last windowMs, and records the request; otherwise returns false. Old timestamps must be cleaned so memory does not grow unbounded. Then show how you would wire it as Express middleware and return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header when blocked. You may use AI tools to build it.
feature.sample: isAllowed('u1') x5 within 60s -> true; 6th call -> false; after 60s window elapses -> true again
feature.hint: Store an array of timestamps per user; filter out entries older than windowMs on each call.

prompt.task: Write a prompt that instructs an AI assistant to summarize a 10-page technical research paper into exactly 3 bullets for a busy CEO — focusing on business impact and risk, not methodology. The model must not invent numbers.
prompt.hint: Specify role, audience, format, and a hallucination guardrail.

prompt.task: Write a prompt for an AI coding assistant to generate a Python script that de-duplicates a 10 million-row CSV on a composite key, running on a machine with only 1 GB of free RAM, without loading the whole file.
prompt.hint: Specify constraints, memory budget, acceptable libraries, and streaming/chunking behaviour.

prompt.task: Write a prompt that makes an AI critique a draft business email for tone, bias, and factual accuracy, returning a strict JSON object with fields {issues[], rewrittenEmail, confidence} and nothing else.
prompt.hint: Specify output format, role, and how to handle uncertainty.
